chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Every app is a stack of three layers
Almost every application you test, whether it's the Bizlevate HRMS, PrimeSales 360 or an appointment booking system, is built in layers. At the top is the UI (the web page or mobile screen a user sees and clicks). In the middle is the API / backend (the server code that receives requests, applies business rules, and decides what to do). At the bottom is the database, where the data actually lives after the user closes the browser.

When you click "Apply Leave" in the HRMS, this happens:

```
[UI]  Employee fills the leave form → clicks Submit
   ↓  HTTP request: POST /api/leave-requests  { leaveTypeId: 2, start: "2026-10-05", end: "2026-10-07" }
[API] Validates: is balance enough? do dates overlap? is the user allowed?
   ↓  SQL: INSERT INTO leave_requests (...) VALUES (...)
[DB]  Row stored in leave_requests with status = 'pending'
   ↑  Returns the new row / success
[API] Sends back { id: 4512, status: "pending" }
[UI]  Shows "Leave request submitted"
```

Notice that the UI only shows what the API says. The API only reports what it believes happened. The database is the source of truth. If the UI shows "Saved" but the row never landed in the table (or landed with a wrong value), only a database check will catch it. That is the whole reason this manual exists.
## Where each testing tool sits in the stack
Selenium and Playwright drive the top layer. They click buttons and read text from the screen. Postman, pytest with requests, and Cypress cy.request work at the middle layer. SQL is your tool for the bottom layer. A mature test strategy verifies all three, and the interesting bugs live in the gaps between them:

| Layer | Tool examples | What it can prove | What it can't prove |
|---|---|---|---|
| UI | Selenium, Playwright, Cypress | The screen looks and behaves right | That data was really stored correctly |
| API | Postman, pytest, REST-assured | The contract and business logic respond correctly | That the DB state matches the response |
| Database | SQL client, SQL inside test code | The real stored state | That the user experience is right |

A UI test that ends with expect(page.getByText('Saved')).toBeVisible() will happily pass even if the backend silently wrote NULL into a salary column. Adding one SQL assertion closes that gap.
## What a relational database actually is
A relational database stores data in tables. Each table is a grid: columns define what kind of information is stored (name, email, hire date), and each row is one record (one employee). Tables are connected through keys. A primary key uniquely identifies each row (employee_id = 101). A foreign key is a column in one table that points to the primary key of another, which is how relationships are represented.

```
departments                    employees
+---------------+----------+   +-------------+-----------+---------------+
| department_id | name     |   | employee_id | full_name | department_id |
+---------------+----------+   +-------------+-----------+---------------+
| 1             | Finance  |   | 101         | Asha K.   | 2             |
| 2             | QA       |   | 102         | Ravi S.   | 2             |
| 3             | HR       |   | 103         | Mina T.   | 1             |
+---------------+----------+   +-------------+-----------+---------------+
```

Employee 101 doesn't store the text "QA". It stores 2, a pointer to the QA row in departments. This avoids repeating data (rename the department once and every employee reflects it), and it lets the database enforce rules such as "you can't assign an employee to a department that doesn't exist." That is called referential integrity, and Part 4 and Part 8 rely on it heavily.
Relational databases also give you transactions and ACID guarantees (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability). In plain words: a group of changes either all happen or none do, and the data doesn't end up half-written. Payroll is the classic example: deducting tax and crediting net pay must succeed together. We cover this properly in 7.3 and 7.7.
## Relational (SQL) vs NoSQL
"NoSQL" is an umbrella term for databases that don't use the table-and-relationship model. There are several families:
Document stores (MongoDB, Couchbase) store JSON-like documents. An employee with their addresses and skills could be a single nested document.
Key-value stores (Redis, DynamoDB in simple mode) map a key to a value. Often used for caching and sessions.
Column-family stores (Cassandra, HBase) are built for huge write volumes across many machines.
Graph databases (Neo4j) store nodes and relationships, good for social networks or recommendation engines.

| Aspect | Relational (SQL) | NoSQL (typical document store) |
|---|---|---|
| Structure | Fixed schema, defined up front | Flexible, each document can differ |
| Relationships | Joins across tables | Usually embedded or referenced manually |
| Consistency | Strong (ACID) by default | Often eventual, varies by product |
| Query language | SQL (standardized-ish) | Product-specific (e.g., MongoDB query syntax) |
| Best for | Structured business data: HR, payroll, orders, bookings | Flexible/variable data, massive scale, caching |

HR, payroll, leave, attendance and appointment systems are highly structured and relationship-heavy (employees → departments → leave requests → approvals), and they need correctness guarantees. That is exactly why they run on relational databases, and it is why this manual is SQL-only. Some products also use both: SQL for core business data and Redis for caching or sessions. If you meet MongoDB on a project later, the thinking in this manual (verify stored state against expected state) transfers even though the query syntax doesn't.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## SQL is the language you use to talk to a relational database
SQL stands for Structured Query Language (people say "sequel" or "S-Q-L", both are fine). It is declarative: you describe what result you want, not how to compute it. In Selenium you write step-by-step instructions (find element, click, wait, read). In SQL you write "give me all employees in QA hired after January 2025" and the database engine decides the fastest way to fetch it.
```sql
SELECT employee_id, first_name, hire_date
FROM   employees
WHERE  department_id = 2
  AND  hire_date > '2025-01-01';
```

## Why dialects exist
SQL has an official standard (ANSI/ISO), but every database vendor implemented it slightly differently and added their own extensions. So we have dialects: MySQL (and MariaDB), PostgreSQL, SQL Server (T-SQL), Oracle (PL/SQL), SQLite. About 80% of what you write, such as SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY and INSERT, works everywhere. The last 20% (limiting rows, string concatenation, date arithmetic, auto-increment columns) differs, and that's where testers get bitten when they copy a query from a blog post.

| Task | MySQL | PostgreSQL | SQL Server |
|---|---|---|---|
| First 5 rows | LIMIT 5 | LIMIT 5 | SELECT TOP 5 ... |
| Current timestamp | NOW() | NOW() | GETDATE() |
| Concatenate | CONCAT(a, ' ', b) | a \|\| ' ' \|\| b | a + ' ' + b or CONCAT() |
| Quote an identifier | `order` (backticks) | "order" (double quotes) | [order] (brackets) |
| Auto-increment key | AUTO_INCREMENT | SERIAL / GENERATED ... AS IDENTITY | IDENTITY(1,1) |
| String aggregation | GROUP_CONCAT() | STRING_AGG() | STRING_AGG() |

Because this manual is for testers who may be on any of the three, every chapter with dialect differences will flag them, and Appendix B collects them in one place. Treat the manual's examples as MySQL-flavoured unless a note says otherwise, and always check what your project actually uses (ask the developer, or look at the connection string; port 3306 is usually MySQL, 5432 PostgreSQL, 1433 SQL Server).
## The five statement families
SQL statements are grouped by what they do. You'll see these acronyms constantly:

| Family | Full name | Purpose | Examples | Tester relevance |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| DQL | Data Query Language | Read data | SELECT | Daily use. This is 80% of tester SQL |
| DML | Data Manipulation Language | Change data | INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE | Test data setup and cleanup (Part 7) |
| DDL | Data Definition Language | Change structure | CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE | Reading migration scripts, awareness (7.4, 6.4) |
| DCL | Data Control Language | Control access | GRANT, REVOKE | Understanding your permissions (0.5) |
| TCL | Transaction Control Language | Group changes | START TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK | Safe experimentation (7.3) |

Some people place SELECT under DML instead of a separate DQL; you'll see both in textbooks. The split isn't important. What matters is the risk gradient: DQL is harmless, DML changes rows, DDL changes the structure itself (and in some databases can't be undone by a rollback), and DCL changes who can do what. A good habit is to feel a small alarm bell when you move from left to right in that table.

chapters.title: 0.3 What Testers Use SQL For
chapters.overviewText: SQL isn't a "nice to have" skill for QA. It's often the difference between a tester who can only validate what's visible on the UI and one who can independently confirm whether the actual data is correct. Most bugs that matter (wrong totals, missing records, orphaned data, incorrect status transitions) don't show up cleanly in the UI. They show up in the database, and SQL is how you get there. Here are the core categories where testers rely on it. The most common use: do something in the UI or API, then check the database. After creating an employee through the onboarding form, does exactly one row appear in employees, with the right department, a status of active, and a non-null created_at?

chapters.contentMarkdown:
SQL isn't a "nice to have" skill for QA. It's often the difference between a tester who can only validate what's visible on the UI and one who can independently confirm whether the actual data is correct. Most bugs that matter (wrong totals, missing records, orphaned data, incorrect status transitions) don't show up cleanly in the UI. They show up in the database, and SQL is how you get there.
Here are the core categories where testers rely on it.
## Confirming that an action really persisted
The most common use: do something in the UI or API, then check the database. After creating an employee through the onboarding form, does exactly one row appear in employees, with the right department, a status of active, and a non-null created_at? UI success messages can lie; rows can't.
```sql
SELECT employee_id, first_name, email, department_id, status, created_at
FROM   employees
WHERE  email = 'asha.qa001@example.com';
```

## Validating what the UI displays, and the calculations behind it
Cross-checking what the application displays against what is actually stored is the single most common QA use case. When a screen shows "Annual leave balance: 12 days," how do you know that's correct? You could recalculate by hand, or you could ask the database. In the sample schema, approved days live in leave_requests and the yearly entitlement lives in leave_types (18 days for Annual):
```sql
SELECT employee_id, SUM(days) AS days_taken
| FROM   leave_requests | WHERE  status = 'approved' | AND  leave_type_id = 1                                   -- Annual | AND  start_date >= '2026-01-01' AND start_date < '2027-01-01' | GROUP BY employee_id; |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| If this returns 8 days taken for an employee, the balance should be 18 − 8 = 10. If the UI shows 12, it is displaying a balance that only makes sense if 6 days were taken. You've just caught a data-integrity bug that no amount of UI clicking would have revealed. | Payroll, leave accrual, attendance hours, appraisal scoring and appointment totals are all computed values, and much of that logic happens entirely in the backend. The UI just displays the result. To test the logic and not just the display, compute the expected value independently in SQL, query the intermediate tables, and compare. | sql | -- Expected net pay according to raw components | SELECT employee_id, |
| basic_salary + allowances - deductions AS expected_net, | net_pay                                AS stored_net | FROM   payroll | WHERE  pay_month = '2026-08-01' | AND  basic_salary + allowances - deductions <> net_pay;   -- any row here is a bug |
```

## Setting up and cleaning up test data
Automated tests (Playwright, Cypress, Selenium) need known starting states. If a test needs "an employee with exactly 3 pending leave requests," it's far more reliable to insert that data directly than to click through the UI three times. UI-based setup is slow, brittle, and itself subject to bugs. Many test frameworks use SQL scripts or ORM-based seeders for exactly this reason. A few statements can also create scenarios that are painful in the UI: a payroll run with a specific mix of statuses, an appointment slot in the past.
sql
-- Setup: 3 pending requests for employee 3 (treated as a test-owned employee here)
```sql
INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days, status) VALUES
(3, 1, '2026-10-05', '2026-10-05', 1, 'pending'),
(3, 1, '2026-10-12', '2026-10-13', 2, 'pending'),
(3, 1, '2026-10-19', '2026-10-21', 3, 'pending');
```
Note that leave_type_id and days are NOT NULL in the sample schema, so the insert must supply them. Teardown works the same way. After the test run, you remove what you inserted so the next run starts fresh:
```sql
DELETE FROM leave_requests
WHERE  employee_id = 3
  AND  status = 'pending';
```
This cleanup is only safe because employee 3 is owned by the test. On a shared database, scope your cleanup to rows you created (tagged IDs, e-mail domains), as described in 0.4. Part 7 covers this in depth.
## Debugging failed tests and investigating bugs
When an automated test fails, the first question is always "is this a real bug, or a data/environment problem?" SQL lets you answer that in seconds. Suppose a Cypress test expects to pick "Sita Rai" from an employee dropdown and fails:
```sql
SELECT employee_id, first_name, last_name, status, is_deleted
FROM   employees
WHERE  first_name = 'Sita' AND last_name = 'Rai';
```
No rows (or is_deleted = 1, or a status of resigned) means the environment simply doesn't have that seed data, or the record is filtered out by design. You've saved yourself from chasing a phantom UI bug.
The same idea applies to bugs a user reports. When a screen looks wrong ("why does this employee show 0 leave balance?"), SQL tells you whether the fault is in the UI, the API, or the data. If the database has the right value, the fault is upstream. If the database has the wrong value, you've narrowed it to backend logic or a bad data load. That single distinction saves hours of back-and-forth with developers.
## Finding hidden data problems
Duplicates, orphaned rows, impossible dates, nulls where there should be values, records stuck in a status. Tests that click through screens rarely find these. Queries do. Part 6 and Part 10 are built around this.
## Verifying migrations, releases and environment differences
Before/after row counts, checksum comparisons and schema comparisons across environments (Part 6). When a bug appears in only one environment, SQL lets you compare row counts, specific records or schema differences between, say, staging and production directly, rather than guessing. Do any comparison involving production through a read-only account or a read replica (11.2).
## Adding DB assertions inside automation
Here is how it looks side by side. A Playwright test with a database check at the end:
```ts
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';
import { Client } from 'pg';
```

| test('creating an employee stores a correct row', async ({ page }) => { | await page.goto('/employees/new'); | await page.getByLabel('First name').fill('Asha'); |
|---|---|---|
| await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('asha.qa001@example.com'); | await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }).click(); | await expect(page.getByText('Employee created')).toBeVisible(); |

| // --- DB assertion: the UI said "created", now prove it --- | const db = new Client({ connectionString: process.env.QA_DB_URL }); | await db.connect(); | const { rows } = await db.query( |
|---|---|---|---|
| 'SELECT first_name, status FROM employees WHERE email = $1', | ['asha.qa001@example.com'] | ); | await db.end(); |

  expect(rows).toHaveLength(1);          // exactly one, no duplicates
| expect(rows[0].first_name).toBe('Asha'); | expect(rows[0].status).toBe('active'); | }); |
|---|---|---|
| The same idea in Selenium with Python: | python | import pymysql |

```py
def test_create_employee(driver):
    # ... UI steps with driver.find_element(...).click() ...
```

    conn = pymysql.connect(host="qa-db", user="qa_readonly", password="...", database="hrms_qa")
```sql
    with conn.cursor() as cur:
        cur.execute("SELECT status FROM employees WHERE email = %s", ("asha.qa001@example.com",))
        rows = cur.fetchall()
    conn.close()
```

    assert len(rows) == 1
## assert rows[0][0] == "active"
Notice the $1 and %s placeholders instead of pasting the email into the string. That is parameterized querying, which avoids quoting bugs and SQL injection. Two practical notes: the Playwright example uses the PostgreSQL client (pg); with MySQL you would use a client such as mysql2, whose placeholder is ?. And because email is unique in the sample schema, a real test should generate a fresh address per run (for example, with a timestamp) or clean up afterwards, otherwise the second run fails for the wrong reason. Part 9 goes deeper on wiring SQL into Playwright, Cypress, pytest and CI.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
This section is about a discipline every QA engineer needs before writing a single query against a real system: understanding what kind of access you have, and what kind you should be using. These are not always the same thing.
## Know which kind of access you have
Read-only access (SELECT only): you can query and view data, but cannot INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or alter the schema. This is the right default for shared environments like staging, and especially production.
Read-write access: you can modify data. This is necessary for test data setup and teardown, and it comes with real risk. An unqualified DELETE or UPDATE (one with no WHERE, or the wrong one) can wipe out or corrupt data that other testers, developers, or even real users depend on.
Never assume which one you have. Check, or ask the DBA or developer:

| sql | -- MySQL: list your own privileges |
|---|---|
| SHOW GRANTS FOR CURRENT_USER(); | -- PostgreSQL: can I update this table? |
| SELECT has_table_privilege('employees', 'UPDATE'); | Why this matters more in QA than you'd think |
| Unlike a developer working in their own local database, QA engineers frequently work in shared environments: staging databases that multiple testers, developers and automated CI pipelines all hit at once. A mistake here doesn't just break your own test. It can break everyone else's tests, invalidate a demo environment (like the one used for the Vatsalya walkthroughs), or, if permissions are misconfigured, touch production data. | Environments and what "safe" means in each |
| Environment | Purpose |
| Typical tester access | Risk of a mistake |
| Dev | Developers' playground |
| Read-write, often | Low, but you may break a dev's work |
| QA / Test | Where you run test cycles |
| Read-write, within agreed rules | Medium: breaks other testers' cycles |
| Staging / UAT | Production-like, final checks and demos |
| Mostly read-only, controlled writes | High: demos and client sign-off depend on it |
| Production | Real users, real money |
| Read-only replica at most, ideally none | Severe: real data, legal/compliance impact |

A staging database used for a client demo (for example, preparing the HRMS demo for a clinic) is a shared, high-visibility asset. An accidental UPDATE there is embarrassing at best and misleading at worst.
## Rules that keep you out of trouble in shared databases
Other testers, developers and automation jobs are using the same data as you. Write down these habits and follow them until they're automatic:
Know your environment before you type. Confirm which database you're actually connected to, using the connection string, the client's connection tab, or a quick query. Running a "safe" test query against what you thought was staging but was actually production is one of the most common and costly QA mistakes.
Look before you change. Run a SELECT with the exact WHERE you plan to use, count the rows, and only then convert it to an UPDATE or DELETE. If it returns 500 rows when you expected 3, you just avoided a disaster.
Never run UPDATE or DELETE without a WHERE. Without it, you affect every row in the table.
Wrap changes in a transaction so you can roll back if the row count surprises you.
Tag your test data so it can be found and cleaned safely: emails like qa_simran_001@example.com or names prefixed QA_, or a dedicated test schema. Then your cleanup WHERE clause targets only your rows.
Don't touch data you didn't create. If a row looks like someone else's, leave it.
Prefer a read replica or a dedicated QA schema for exploratory queries (11.2).
Watch your client's auto-commit setting. In many tools, each statement commits instantly unless you turn auto-commit off.

| sql | -- Which database am I on? |
|---|---|
| -- MySQL | SELECT DATABASE(), @@hostname; |
| -- PostgreSQL | SELECT current_database(), inet_server_addr(); |
| -- SQL Server | SELECT DB_NAME(), @@SERVERNAME; |
| The safe-change workflow, in code | sql |
| -- Step 1: look at exactly what you're about to change | SELECT employee_id, email, status |
| FROM   employees | WHERE  email LIKE 'qa\_simran\_%@example.com'; |

```sql
-- Step 2: open a transaction (MySQL syntax)
START TRANSACTION;
```

```sql
-- Step 3: run the change with the same WHERE
UPDATE employees
SET    status = 'inactive'
WHERE  email LIKE 'qa\_simran\_%@example.com';
```

```sql
-- Step 4: check how many rows were touched (MySQL)
SELECT ROW_COUNT();
```

```sql
-- Step 5: verify, then decide
SELECT employee_id, email, status FROM employees WHERE email LIKE 'qa\_simran\_%@example.com';
COMMIT;      -- happy with it
-- ROLLBACK; -- or undo everything
```
If Step 4 says 3 and you expected 3, commit. If it says 4,200, you just avoided a disaster. Dialect notes: PostgreSQL opens a transaction with BEGIN and reports the affected count itself (for example UPDATE 3); SQL Server uses BEGIN TRANSACTION and @@ROWCOUNT. In MySQL you can also enable a guard rail with SET sql_safe_updates = 1;, which refuses UPDATE/DELETE statements that have no key-based WHERE or LIMIT.
One caution: in MySQL, DDL statements like ALTER TABLE and DROP TABLE cause an implicit commit, so you can't roll them back. PostgreSQL allows transactional DDL, which is friendlier. This is one reason DDL deserves extra respect (7.4).
## Automation and the access boundary
Automation adds a new risk. A UI script that runs 500 times a night against a shared database can create thousands of rows. Give automation its own data prefix and its own cleanup step, and never point a test suite at a database URL you haven't double-checked, because an environment variable that silently defaults to staging is a classic incident.
This is also where the read-only/read-write distinction maps directly onto how frameworks are configured. In Cypress or Playwright suites, CI pipelines typically get credentials scoped to an isolated test database with full read-write access, kept separate from staging and production. That is intentional: it lets automated setup and teardown scripts run freely without risk to shared environments. Against shared QA or staging, automation should be limited to read-only assertions, or tightly scoped writes with an agreed data prefix. When you write SQL-backed setup helpers for Playwright or Cypress (Part 7 and Part 9), this boundary decides whether a helper is safe to run in CI or only safe to run manually against your own sandbox.

A role is a named bundle of privileges you can assign to many users, so you don't grant permissions one person at a time. This follows the principle of least privilege: give each user only the access they need.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Databases have their own users, separate from app users
The employee who logs into the HRMS is an application user, stored in a table like users. A database user is an account the database itself knows about, used by applications, DBAs and testers to connect. The application usually connects with one powerful service account. You should connect with your own account, which has only what you need.
## Permissions are granted per object and per action
Permissions (also called privileges) say who can do what on which object: SELECT on employees, INSERT on attendance, and so on. A role is a named bundle of privileges you can assign to many users, so you don't grant permissions one person at a time. This follows the principle of least privilege: give each user only the access they need.

| Typical role setups: | Role | Can do | Who gets it |
|---|---|---|---|
| qa_readonly | SELECT on the QA/staging schema | Most testers | qa_writer |
| SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE on QA schema | Testers seeding data on QA | app_service | What the app needs, usually no DDL |
| The application itself | dba_admin | Everything | DBAs |

| How permissions are granted | MySQL: |
|---|---|
| CREATE USER 'qa_readonly'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY 'a-strong-password'; | GRANT SELECT ON hrms_qa.* TO 'qa_readonly'@'%'; |

-- See what an account can do
```sql
SHOW GRANTS FOR 'qa_readonly'@'%';
```

PostgreSQL:
```sql
CREATE ROLE qa_readonly LOGIN PASSWORD 'a-strong-password';
GRANT CONNECT ON DATABASE hrms_qa TO qa_readonly;
GRANT USAGE   ON SCHEMA public   TO qa_readonly;
GRANT SELECT  ON ALL TABLES IN SCHEMA public TO qa_readonly;
```

You typically won't run these yourself, since a DBA will. But knowing them helps you ask for the right thing: "please give me SELECT on the QA schema" is a much better request than "please give me DB access."
## How a permission problem looks
MySQL:      ERROR 1142 (42000): UPDATE command denied to user 'qa_readonly'@'10.0.0.5' for table 'employees'
## PostgreSQL: ERROR:  permission denied for table employees

These aren't bugs. They confirm that your access is limited, which is what you want on staging. If your read-only account can modify data, that itself is a finding worth reporting.
## Why this matters beyond your own safety
Permissions are also a testing target. Test that a low-privilege account can't read salary tables, and that the app's service account can't DROP tables. Sensitive columns (salary, national ID, bank details) may be restricted or masked, which ties into PII handling in 7.6. And when you use credentials inside automation (Playwright, pytest, CI), use a read-only account stored in environment variables or a secrets manager, never hard-coded in the repo (11.2 and 9.4 return to this).

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## One small database used throughout the manual
Every example in this manual uses the same compact HRMS and appointment schema, so you can copy any query and run it. Here is the core set. The full version with more seed data is in 12.1, and Appendix E has the ER overview.

| Table | What it holds | departments | Company departments |
|---|---|---|---|
| employees | Staff, with a self-referencing manager_id | leave_types | Annual, Sick, Casual, and so on |
| leave_requests | Requests with status workflow | attendance | Daily check-in/check-out |
| payroll | Monthly pay per employee | services, customers, appointments | The appointment-booking side |

The core schema (MySQL flavour)
```sql
CREATE DATABASE hrms_practice;
USE hrms_practice;
```

| CREATE TABLE departments ( | department_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, |
|---|---|
| name          VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL UNIQUE | ); |

| CREATE TABLE employees ( | employee_id   INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, |
|---|---|
| first_name    VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL, | last_name     VARCHAR(50)  NOT NULL, |
| email         VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL UNIQUE, | department_id INT, |
| manager_id    INT NULL, | hire_date     DATE NOT NULL, |
| status        ENUM('active','inactive','resigned') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'active', | is_deleted    TINYINT(1) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, |
| created_at    TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, | FOREIGN KEY (department_id) REFERENCES departments(department_id), |
| FOREIGN KEY (manager_id)    REFERENCES employees(employee_id) | ); |

```sql
CREATE TABLE leave_types (
```
| leave_type_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, | name          VARCHAR(30) NOT NULL, |
|---|---|
| days_per_year INT NOT NULL | ); |

| CREATE TABLE leave_requests ( | leave_request_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, |
|---|---|
| employee_id      INT NOT NULL, | leave_type_id    INT NOT NULL, |
| start_date       DATE NOT NULL, | end_date         DATE NOT NULL, |
| days             DECIMAL(4,1) NOT NULL, | status           ENUM('pending','approved','rejected','cancelled') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'pending', |
| approved_by      INT NULL, | created_at       TIMESTAMP DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP, |
| FOREIGN KEY (employee_id)   REFERENCES employees(employee_id), | FOREIGN KEY (leave_type_id) REFERENCES leave_types(leave_type_id), |
| FOREIGN KEY (approved_by)   REFERENCES employees(employee_id) | ); |

| CREATE TABLE attendance ( | attendance_id INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, | employee_id   INT NOT NULL, |
|---|---|---|
| work_date     DATE NOT NULL, | check_in      TIME NULL, | check_out     TIME NULL, |
| FOREIGN KEY (employee_id) REFERENCES employees(employee_id), | UNIQUE (employee_id, work_date) | ); |

```sql
CREATE TABLE payroll (
```
| payroll_id   INT AUTO_INCREMENT PRIMARY KEY, | employee_id  INT NOT NULL, | pay_month    DATE NOT NULL, | basic_salary DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL, | allowances   DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| deductions   DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0, | net_pay      DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL, | status       ENUM('draft','processed','paid') NOT NULL DEFAULT 'draft', | FOREIGN KEY (employee_id) REFERENCES employees(employee_id) | ); |

A little seed data
```sql
INSERT INTO departments (name) VALUES ('Finance'), ('QA'), ('HR');
```

```sql
INSERT INTO employees (first_name, last_name, email, department_id, manager_id, hire_date) VALUES
('Asha', 'Karki',  'asha@example.com',  2, NULL, '2024-03-01'),
('Ravi', 'Shrestha','ravi@example.com', 2, 1,    '2025-03-10'),
('Mina', 'Thapa',  'mina@example.com',  1, NULL, '2023-07-15');
```

```sql
INSERT INTO leave_types (name, days_per_year) VALUES ('Annual', 18), ('Sick', 12);
```

```sql
INSERT INTO leave_requests (employee_id, leave_type_id, start_date, end_date, days, status) VALUES
(2, 1, '2026-10-05', '2026-10-07', 3, 'pending');
```

Verify your setup with a first query
```sql
SELECT e.first_name, d.name AS department
FROM   employees e
JOIN   departments d ON d.department_id = e.department_id;
```

If you see three rows, you're ready.
Ways to run it
Docker (fastest, nothing to install permanently):
```sql
 docker run --name sql-practice -e MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD=root -p 3306:3306 -d mysql:8
Then connect with a client on localhost:3306. For PostgreSQL, use postgres:16 with -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=root -p 5432:5432.
```
Local install: MySQL Community Server with MySQL Workbench, or PostgreSQL with pgAdmin.
A universal client: DBeaver connects to all three dialects and is the one I'd suggest if you'll bounce between databases.
Browser-only: an online SQL playground (fine for Parts 1–5, but not for permissions and transactions practice).
Practice on your own machine or a throwaway database, never on a shared QA or staging one, until you're comfortable with Part 7.

chapters.contentMarkdown:
## Being clear about scope
This manual teaches SQL as a QA tool, the SQL a tester needs to verify, investigate and prepare data. It deliberately leaves out areas that belong to other roles or deserve their own books. Knowing where the edge is prevents surprise and points you to the right next resource.
## Topics intentionally left out
Database administration: installing servers, backups and restores, replication setup, user management at scale, capacity planning. (0.5 only covers what you need to understand about permissions.)
Database design and normalization theory: we touch schema patterns in 8.4, but not normal forms, ER modelling as a design discipline, or designing a schema from scratch.
Writing stored procedures, triggers and functions: 8.3 teaches you to read and test them, not build complex ones.
Deep performance tuning: 8.5 covers EXPLAIN and spotting slow queries so you can escalate with evidence, not index strategy or query-planner internals.
NoSQL query languages: MongoDB, Redis and others are mentioned in 0.1 only for context.
Data warehousing and BI: OLAP, star schemas, ETL tool development. Part 6 covers validating ETL output with SQL, not building pipelines.
ORMs and application code: Hibernate, Sequelize, Prisma and so on. You'll see SQL that these generate, but not how to configure them.
Security testing beyond basics: 9.7 introduces SQL injection so testers can recognize and report it. Full penetration testing is a separate discipline.
Load and performance testing: database behaviour under stress is a specialist topic.
## Where to go next
If your work grows toward any of these, the natural follow-ups are: a proper database-design course (normalization, indexing), your database vendor's official documentation (MySQL Reference Manual, PostgreSQL docs, Microsoft T-SQL docs), a data engineering or analytics path (which fits well with the data analytics learning you already do), and API and automation manuals like your Postman, pytest, Cypress and Playwright material, where Part 9 of this manual acts as the bridge.
